Blue Owl just logged a record fundraising quarter and lifted assets under management 12% to nearly $330 billion, even as its stock is down about 35% this year as investors stay jumpy about private credit.

Blue Owl, an alternative asset manager, said it raised $12.6 billion of new capital commitments in the third quarter, bringing its past-12-month total to $48.8 billion. It also reported slightly higher profit, with adjusted distributable earnings per share rising to 24 cents from 22 cents a year earlier, Reuters reported.

e committed money is actually invested, not when a client signs the check, so there can be a lag between headline commitments and fee growth.

That gap is getting more attention while private credit faces tougher questions on risk. Blue Owl’s credit business originated $5.2 billion of direct loans in the quarter, yet overall deployment fell by $300 million, which can leave more cash uninvested and earning little. Meanwhile, the stock market is also trying to price what happens if a weaker economy or overstretched borrowers leads to higher loan losses, which can weigh on listed direct lenders even when fundraising looks strong.

AUM growth can look great on paper, but shareholders ultimately care about earnings. With alternative managers, earnings depend on when committed capital gets put to work and starts generating management fees, so slower deployment can mean “cash drag” and delayed revenue.

At the same time, listed private-credit managers can trade like a referendum on credit risk. If investors think defaults and recovery values might worsen, they may keep pressure on the shares until there’s evidence that new deals are being deployed at attractive loan yields without setting up future losses. That’s why Blue Owl’s fundraising strength and share performance can diverge for a while.
